title: Be Holy, and Love Your Neighbor
summary: God calls the whole congregation to be holy because he is holy, and then spells out what that means in dozens of short commands covering family, worship, harvest, business, courts, speech, the treatment of the disabled, the elderly, and foreigners, and the rejection of pagan mourning and occult practices. At the center stands the command to love your neighbor as yourself, later extended to the foreigner. The refrain "I am the LORD" runs through the chapter, grounding every command in God's own character.
story: Leviticus 18 told Israel what not to be: unlike Egypt and Canaan. Chapter 19 turns to what Israel is to be, and it does so with the widest range of any chapter in the book. It is addressed to "the whole congregation of Israel" (verse 2), not only the priests, and it treats holiness as something that reaches into fields, markets, courtrooms, and conversations as much as into the sanctuary. Many readers consider it the heart of the Holiness Code (chapters 17 to 26) and one of the peaks of the Old Testament's ethics. Chapter 20 will return to some of these matters with penalties attached.
historical:
The chapter assumes a settled farming life that Israel did not yet have in the wilderness: fields to harvest, vineyards to glean, fruit trees to plant, hired workers, courts, and markets with weights and measures. Verse 23 says as much ("When you enter the land"). As with the rest of Leviticus, traditional readers see these as laws given at Sinai in anticipation of settlement, while many critical scholars date the Holiness Code's final form to the late monarchy or the exile. The practices it forbids were real features of the world around Israel. Cutting the body in grief is attested among Israel's neighbors, and the prophets of Baal gash themselves in 1 Kings 18:28. Mediums who consulted the dead appear in the story of Saul at Endor (1 Samuel 28), where the same Hebrew word as verse 31 is used. The gleaning laws of verses 9 and 10 are what allow Ruth, a Moabite widow, to gather grain in the field of Boaz (Ruth 2).

The command to love one's neighbor was already treated as central in Jewish teaching before and alongside the New Testament. Rabbi Akiva, in the early second century AD, is remembered as calling it a great principle of the Torah, and a generation before Jesus, Hillel summarized the law with a negative form of the same rule, that one should not do to a neighbor what one hates.
cultural:
Many of the commands protect people with little power. The poor and the foreigner were to glean what the harvesters left at the edges of the field and what fell in the vineyard, a kind of welfare built into ownership itself. Day laborers lived hand to mouth, so their wages were due the same evening (verse 13). The deaf could not hear a curse and the blind could not see a stumbling block, which made them easy targets; the law says God sees what they cannot (verse 14). Courts were to be impartial in both directions, favoring neither the poor out of pity nor the rich out of fear. The elderly were to be honored by rising in their presence. Honest weights mattered in a world without standard measures, where merchants often kept two sets of stones for buying and selling.

Some commands puzzle modern readers because their symbolism is lost to us. The ban on mixing two kinds of livestock, seed, or fabric (verse 19) seems to mirror the created order of Genesis 1, where things are made "according to their kinds", and the separation between Israel and the nations. The fruit of a young tree was treated like an uncircumcised foreskin for three years, then given to God in the fourth, and only then eaten. Verses 20 to 22, concerning an enslaved woman promised to another man, assume the slavery of the ancient world; they spare both from the death penalty that applied to adultery with a free woman promised in marriage, "because she had not been freed" (verse 20), and require the man to bring a guilt offering.
literary: The chapter is built from short commands, most ending with "I am the LORD" or "I am the LORD your God", which occurs about fifteen times after the opening call to holiness. The effect is a litany: each rule is signed with God's name. Jewish interpreters have long noticed that the chapter echoes most of the Ten Commandments (honoring parents, the Sabbath, idols, stealing, lying, God's name), set among newer and more specific laws. Ritual and ethical commands are mixed without apology, so that eating a peace offering on time and paying a worker on time stand side by side. The chapter also builds in pairs: "love your neighbor as yourself" in verse 18 is echoed in verse 34, where the foreigner is to be loved "as yourself" too, because Israel knew what it was to be a foreigner in Egypt.

outline.t: Be holy: parents, Sabbaths, and no idols
Leave the gleanings for the poor and the foreigner
Honesty, justice, and love for the neighbor
Mixtures, an enslaved woman, and young fruit trees
No divination, pagan mourning rites, or mediums
The elderly, the foreigner, and honest measures

doctrines.note: Verse 2 grounds Israel's holiness in God's: be holy because I am holy. Holiness here is not withdrawal from ordinary life but a way of living in it: how you harvest, pay workers, speak, judge, and treat strangers.

The chapter shows that the law is not only ritual. It weaves worship and ethics together and summarizes its concern for others in a single sentence, love your neighbor as yourself, which Jesus and the apostles would call the summary of the law's duties toward people.

Every command is signed with God's name, so the chapter is also a portrait of the God behind it: one who cares about the deaf and the blind, the poor at the edge of the field, the worker waiting for wages, and the foreigner who has no family to protect him.

words.note: Qadosh, holy. The basic sense is set apart, belonging to God and marked off from common use. Applied to God, it names his utter distinctness and moral purity. Applied to Israel, it means a people set apart for him, and this chapter shows that being set apart is displayed in justice and kindness as much as in ritual.

Ahav, to love. It is used in verse 18 for the neighbor and in verse 34 for the foreigner. In the Old Testament love is more than a feeling; it is loyal, practical commitment. The context of verse 18 (no hatred in the heart, no revenge, no grudge, honest rebuke) shows that it governs inner attitudes as well as actions.

Rea, neighbor or fellow. In its immediate context it refers to a fellow Israelite, which is why verse 34 explicitly extends the same love to the foreigner. The question of who counts as a neighbor is the one a lawyer later put to Jesus, which led to the parable of the Good Samaritan.

Ger, the foreigner or resident alien: someone living in Israel without the land, family ties, or legal standing of a native. The chapter names him with the poor in the gleaning law and commands that he be loved as oneself. The reason given is memory: Israel had been foreigners in Egypt.

christ: When Jesus was asked which commandment was most important, he joined Deuteronomy 6:5 to this chapter: "The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these" (Mark 12:31). When a lawyer asked "And who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29), Jesus told of a Samaritan, a member of a despised group, who showed mercy to a wounded Jew, and so stretched the command in the direction verse 34 already pointed. In the Sermon on the Mount he went further still, telling his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44). Paul (Romans 13:9 and Galatians 5:14) and James (James 2:8) each call this verse the summary of the law. Peter quotes verse 2, "Be holy, because I am holy" (1 Peter 1:16), as a call to Christians. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who lived this chapter completely, and his people as those who are called to it again by his Spirit.

hard.q: Why is a ban on mixed fabrics listed next to love your neighbor, and how do Christians decide which of these laws still apply?
hard.a: This is a fair question, and the chapter itself refuses to separate ritual from ethics. Christians have answered it in several ways. A long tradition, found in Thomas Aquinas and John Calvin and in many Protestant confessions, divides the law into moral, civil, and ceremonial parts: the moral law (love of neighbor, honesty, justice) remains binding, while ceremonial laws like the mixtures of verse 19 pointed to Israel's separateness and were fulfilled in Christ, and civil laws governed Israel as a nation. Others argue that the Mosaic law as a whole was a covenant with Israel that has been fulfilled in Christ, and that Christians are bound by its commands as they are taken up and reshaped in the New Testament, which is where love of neighbor reappears and the mixture laws do not. Jewish tradition, by contrast, treats all these commands as binding on Jews, and observant Jews still avoid garments mixing wool and linen (as Deuteronomy 22:11 specifies). All sides agree that verse 19 had a meaning for Israel, most likely a visible reminder of order and separation, even if its application has changed.

questions: This chapter places paying a worker on time beside keeping the Sabbath. Which parts of your ordinary economic life do you think of as outside the reach of holiness?
The command to love your neighbor comes right after commands not to hold a grudge or seek revenge. Who is the neighbor this verse is hardest for you to love?
Israel was told to love the foreigner because it remembered being foreign in Egypt. What memories of your own weakness or need might make you more generous toward others?
